utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The case number IT-97-24-PT. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the Prosecution, I am Michael Keegan, assisted by Ms Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tell us again with the microphone on so it is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Vucicevic, on behalf of the defendant, today with Defence is appearing Professor Anthony D'Amato of Chicago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can the accused hear in a language that he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two motions which the Chamber has before it today. The first is the Prosecution motion to amend. There is some problem with the mechanics. (Pause). The position, as I understand it, is that the simultaneous transcription is, of course, being made but it is not showing on the screens and it does not seem to me necessary that it should, so we will proceed. I was saying that there were the two motions: one from each party. It would seem sensible to start with the motion to amend. We will consider the other motion in due course. Mr Keegan, that is your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour. The Prosecutor, as indicated in her submission of 28th January, respectfully requests leave to amend the indictment in the subject case, for the purposes of adding counts 2 through 15 to the indictment. I assume, having not actually heard anything but getting the official copy, that our request to file the reply was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will, for the purposes of this argument, we will certainly accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. In which case I will endeavour not to repeat anything in the reply in my submissions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I have not received a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you not received a copy Mr D'Amato?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you use the microphone, please, and tell us the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: We have not received a copy of the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must have a copy. We will hear what the Prosecutor has to say. Then, if you want an opportunity to study the document, of course, you shall have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I presume it is in the mail box for the Defence downstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr Keegan, I understand that one of my colleagues does not have it either, but it has been handed in. Do we have a copy? In those circumstances, Mr Keegan, it may be just as well if you would refer to that document and go through it, briefly indicating your argument on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The nature of the reply, your Honour, was of course a reply to the Defence response to the Prosecutor's request for leave to amend. In substance, the position of the Prosecutor is, first, that the Article 9(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights is inapposite here. That provision of the Covenant is focused on insuring the right to personal liberty; that is, the province of unlawful arrest and detention. The notice requirement under Article 9(2) is focused solely on that issue. In this case, this accused was lawfully arrested, pursuant to an arrest warrant issued as a result of a confirmed indictment. Upon his arrest, he was notified of the reasons for his arrest and given a copy of the indictment in his own language. Subsequent to that time, as this Chamber well knows, he has certainly exercised his right to challenge the lawfulness of his pre-trial detention. The notification to the accused and the service of the indictment upon him at the time of arrest, satisfied the requirements of Article 9(2) and that ends the application of that particular provision. The Defence attempt to transpose that notice requirement in Article 9 into some larger limitation on the right of the Prosecution, or even conceivably the court, to amend an indictment at a later date is misguided and incorrect. The right to amend indictments is recognised by every jurisdiction. In each matter, the question of the amendment is generally judged against one particular criterion and that is, as mentioned in our reply, whether there would be substantial prejudice to the right of an accused to a fair trial or, as it might be phrased in the United Kingdom, whether there would be injustice to the accused as a result of the amendment. In our circumstances, given the provisions of Rule 50, which, as a result of an amendment, would restart the pre-trial clock, the 60-day clock, if you will, and the rights of the accused pursuant to Rule 72, to challenge both the indictment both as to its form and substance through pre-trial motions, sufficiently to protect the rights of the accused in this matter. The right of the accused to prepare and present to defence similarly would not be substantially impaired by this amendment. The additional charges arise out of the same basic circumstances and facts as the original indictment and there would be ample time, if necessary, for the Defence to conduct its investigation. The obligation of the Prosecution in this matter is not simply to lay any charge against an accused but the most appropriate charges which he believes best reflects the conduct of the accused. In this matter, both the international community and the accused have the right to a fair trial. The question of a trial without undue delay or speedy trial as the Defence refers to it is also a basic right in every system. Undue delay is relative to the processes of each system and the circumstances of each particular case. It is a fact that history will not judge us by how quickly we conducted our cases here but how just our system and our judgements are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr Keegan, I think you must address the question of delay in this case. The history is this: this accused was arrested in July of last year, the indictment having been reviewed and confirmed as long ago as March last year. The position is this: a year, or nearly a year, after the indictment was reviewed and confirmed, and some six to seven months after the arrest of the defendant, you now seek to amend the indictment. This amendment is not the addition of a count or something of that sort; it involves what is, in effect, the substitution of a new indictment. Now, the question of delay is clearly important. There is an obligation, of course, for a trial to be fair, but there is also an obligation for it to be expeditious. With this sort of delay, how can the Prosecution justify an amendment at this late stage? I say "you"; of course, the criticism is not directed at you personally, Mr Keegan, but, at the Prosecution generally. How is it you could justify such a delay in a case of this sort?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think, as I indicated earlier, that in each case the question of undue delay must be looked at in terms of the processes of the particular system itself, as well as the circumstances of each case. In this case there are, in fact, a number of circumstances which have impacted on the decision of when to submit an amendment. As is clear from the amendment we indicated at the earliest stage of our intention to amend the indictment. In fact we notified counsel at our first meeting of that intent and the basic nature of the articles and the concept we would include in an amendment for the purposes of providing notice. Of course, in the early days of this case, we had a change of Trial Chambers which negated the delay of motions which were already existing which were transposed to this Chamber. We had a question of whether the accused was going to submit to an interrogation, which he ultimately chose not to do, which is his right, but that would also affect the question of when to bring forth an amendment. Then there was the issue of the accused's request for release from pre-trial detention based on the allegations of his serious medical condition. This office already had, in fact, experience in the case of General Dzukic, with an accused who did arrive who did, in fact, end up being terminally ill and was released as a result of that. In that case also there was a pending amendment, but it was prudent to wait until the decision on provisional release based on health was issued and we, in fact, made that statement to this Chamber and to the Defence as early as the beginning of October, if I recall correctly, that we preferred to wait until after the issue of provisional release was determined. Because in our view, if the accused was released based on the seriousness of his medical condition it would directly impact on whether or not there was any purpose in an amendment. There are a number of factors which weigh in the decision; whether this Trial Chamber accepts all of those or any of those as relevant criteria, of course, is your decision. The point is, as I indicated, the crux of the determination at this point, we believe, whether or not the grant of the amendment would have substantial prejudice or result in injustice to this accused with regard to his right to a fair trial. We submit it would not, because of the fact that we are still in the pre-trial stage and the protections that Rule 50 gives by virtue of restarting the clock to the accused and his right to challenge this indictment, because there are two separate stages here: one is the question of the confirmation of the proposed indictment; the second would be whether any or all of that indictment survives challenges by the accused, if they so bring them by virtue of Rule 72, or what other motions they may bring with respect to jurisdiction and other issues. There are many issues still to be resolved here that may affect the ultimate trial. The question here is whether this accused would still have -- be able to achieve a fair trial under our processes with the grant of the amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You, no doubt, say that any unfairness to the accused could be cured by an adjournment of the trial sufficient so that his Defence could be prepared. There are two points about that: the first is that the adjournment, given the size of the amendment which you are asking for, would have to be for a considerable time. Mr D'Amato in his brief speaks of seven months. That does not seem unreasonable, given the size of the case. That means that we would be looking at a trial, if the amendment were to be granted, in October, the accused having been arrested last July. Now, that cannot be expeditious. Therefore, there is a distinction between producing a trial that would be fair to both sides and one that is expeditious. The second point, one that Mr D'Amato makes in his brief, is because there has been such a delay in producing these amendments, the Defence have not had the opportunity which they would otherwise have had of gathering evidence and preparing for an amended indictment which contains all these new counts. Now, that is a potential unfairness, is it not, and one that cannot be cured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If those were, in fact, the circumstances, your Honour, yes, that would result in injustice to the accused. But for the same reason which the Trial Chamber may challenge the Prosecution's assertions as to length of delay, resources needed or any other aspect of its preparation of a case, relative to the right of the accused to an expeditious trial, we believe the Trial Chamber can challenge the Defence to substantiate its assertions. There is a question whether or not another seven months is necessary. All the additional charges flow from the basic facts and circumstances as to genocide. The nature of proof involved in a genocide count will flow over into all of these charges. If you look at the nature of the indictment, the background facts and the preparatory facts for each of the charges, all relate back to the same basic circumstances which occurred in Prijedor. This Defence team has been to Prijedor on a number of occasions already, conducting defences, as they indicated in their communications with this Chamber and with the Prosecution. Certainly, they now understand the nature of the witnesses who were prepared to testify both as to the accused's actions, his character and all the other related factors which would are been necessary for Defence in -- for the genocide charge. Those factors are still going to be applicable to these additional charges. A factor that also plays into the right or the obligation of the Prosecution is, unlike state jurisdictions where the police and prosecution and court, as arms of the state have great control over all aspects of the investigations and the accused, the OTP and in fact the Trial Chamber, in some respects, do not have that same type of leverage of authority. We believe in making determinations about what is undue delay or what is reasonable in light of the circumstances, one must account for the changing opportunity that are available to the Prosecution in its investigations, including the ebb and flow of state communication. The Office of the Prosecutor is continuing to investigate this case, like every other case, up until the end. We will continue to investigate up to the date of final judgement, as is our obligation, because of the nature of this jurisdiction. This factors into the question of timing of the submission of an amendment. If there are other justifications for delays, like the issue of the provisional release here, which was a real question for many months, it is a question for the Prosecutor to decide whether it is appropriate to issue an amendment at a particular time or to continue investigation to see what that evidence may develop with respect to the charges. All those factors we believe should be considered in the question of whether it is undue delay. In this circumstance, how much more time is necessary for the Defence to complete its preparation of its defence, given the related nature of the facts which form the basis of all of these charges. Many of the charges, of course, if they were in a state jurisdiction, would probably, as a result of a Statute lessor, included defences and would have been natural alternative charges in jurisdictions to begin with. We do not have that here. One cannot make that as a blanket statement, but if one looks at the amendments, one would certainly see that, for example, the homicide, the murder offences, the other serious bodily injury offences would in many jurisdictions be related offences to the same or similar facts. I think all those factors which exist in other jurisdictions which do not exist here should be considered in those questions about whether there is undue delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One other matter I want to raise with you is this: it might be argued that the amendment was delayed because of the difficulty of obtaining evidence, or the fact that you had not the evidence to file your amendment. But, as far as I can see, most of the supporting material is evidence which you had in your hands before the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it is not a case where you are saying that there is new material which has come to light which has caused us to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I am suggesting opportunities opened up which might render better or alternative forms of evidence. For example, if we now come into possession of documents in the last recent months, that would supplant witness testimony which would be the necessary form of information. For the purposes of an indictment that might be the preferable form to submit with the indictment, reducing the risk of exposure of a witness prior to the commitment of a trial. So, I am simply saying that the purpose of a continuing investigation simply raises or opens up the options available to the Prosecutor in reaching her determinations. Yes, you are absolutely right. We processed prior to the last few months the information necessary for the amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why was the matter not tended to more quickly? As I have said, in effect, you are substituting a new indictment. This could have been done a very long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that, your Honour, that I can make, is that it was the best judgement of the members of the Prosecution given our experience over the last four years, that, given the other issues in this case that were going on at the beginning, that it was preferable to continue the investigation and wait and see what would happen with the accused in the initial stages, whether he would be released or not, before we submitted the amended indictment. At the time when it became clear he would remain in custody, we then submitted. We made our intentions clear back in October, as early as I can recall. Prior to that, the notice we intended to amend had been made from the very beginning days to give the Defence -- to put them on notice that they would have the opportunity to act accordingly. Presumably a prudent Defence counsel when making trips to Prijedor, knowing the intentions of the Prosecution, is going to act accordingly. We believe those are relevant questions for the court also to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whether prudent Defence counsel could have anticipated such a large-scale change in the indictment, I do not know. I rather doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Our discussions were fairly candid. We made it clear we intended including the charges that are there, from our very first meeting. I was simply going to move on to Rule 50, if you would like to ask questions at this stage, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With respect to the actual confirmation process, your Honour, Rule 50 -- the amended Rule 50 because, of course, it has changed since we began this case and in fact since the Defence raised its motion for clarification under Rule 50 -- the revised Rule 50 addresses only the mechanics for the amendment of an indictment dependent on the status of the indictment and of the accused. It does not alter the standard or the manner of review of the -- or the obligation of the confirming judges if it is before the Chamber. That obligation is still derived from Article 19 of the Statute and Rule 47 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Article 19 indicates that if a judge is satisfied that a prima facie case exists, he or she shall confirm the indictment. Neither Article 19, Rule 47, nor Rule 50 make any provision for the right of an accused to contest the confirmation process or the supporting material. Under Rule 50(A), by its language, that after initial appearance the request for leave to amend should be done by way of motion, would indicate that the Defence has an apparent right to comment upon or object to the request for leave, itself. At that stage -- that is, the nature of the objection only being to the request for leave to amend and not to the substance of the indictment itself -- the only viable objection from the Defence is that the very fact of an amendment itself will substantially prejudice the right of an accused to a fair trial. That should be the only question here. Absent such a finding, the Trial Chamber should then move on to the confirmation process in which it is guided by Article 19 and Rule 47. Interestingly, reading of Article 19 and the two Rules I mentioned, raise the issue of whether a judge can deny a confirmation for any reason once he or she is satisfied there is a prima facie case. If a judge cannot deny a confirmation for any reason other than lack of a prima facie case it then is clear that the right of an accused to object flows directly from the right of an accused to a fair trial. That would be handled through Rule 72, preliminary motions, by way of objection to the form or substance of an indictment. We believe, however, that all of the factors we have discussed prior would be necessary for the court to consider prior to making a determination of whether the very fact of leave to amend would substantially prejudice the right of an accused to a fair trial. It is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that in a situation of a post-appearance request for leave to amend, post-initial appearance, that the Defence has absolutely no right to receive the supporting material or to object to the basis of the indictment at confirmation. That is consistent with the confirmation process under Rule 47 in the other two instances under the Rules, which are, of course, prior to the time an indictment is actually confirmed or the appearance prior to an initial appearance of the accused. In this case, we provided the materials to the Defence with our request for leave to amend because of the background in this case. The Defence had clearly made it an issue from the early days. Rather than go through what would have been the obvious motion to provide the materials had we not done so, in an effort to simply speed up the process, we provided them. But it is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor, as we have done in other cases pending before the Chambers, that they have no right to the materials nor any right to comment on the confirmation process, itself. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Keegan. Now, who is going to deal with this on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we split the argument?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. Then I will address the objection to the leave to amend, which Mr Keegan says at least relevant under the fact that this is a motion to amend. Mr Keegan has referred to the conversations we had and I was very happy to have those conversations back in September and to receive all the supporting materials and I thanked him for that. I think the openness and transparency of the trial is a great asset, and I wanted to work very closely with the Prosecution. I was not ever going to comment on our conversations, on the substance of our conversations, because I felt that those were off the record. But since Mr Keegan has commented on them rather fulsomely right now, let me rise to object to some of the things he said. First of all, he said that he made it very clear to us that these new counts he was going to add; that is not so. All he told me was that they were thinking of adding a count of a crime against humanity. When I pressed him on that he said "well, maybe persecution", but certainly not 14 new counts. It got no more specific than that. Secondly, the idea that the Prosecution was entitled to continue to delay to amend the indictment because of conversations we were having and because of the defendant's physical condition; not so. I think the Prosecution was holding over our head the threat of a vague possibility of an avalanche of amendments in order to either get us to cooperate with the Prosecution -- which I was not against in principle -- or to keep us off balance. This was a tactic, it was not the neutral situation that Mr Keegan suggests. It was a way of holding something over our head which we did not know about, but which they knew. Since he has admitted that all the facts were there -- all the facts he needed to make the indictment -- it seems that the only reason that he did not add these new counts to the indictment were for tactical reasons, for negotiating reasons to keep us off balance, perhaps to investigate the situation in Prijedor without us knowing what he was going, looking for, because we had no idea what the counts were. Those are pathologies which result from a failure to get Article 9 seriously. I will get to Article 9 in just a minute, but before that I want to just make a few other comments on Mr Keegan's statements. He said that all these additional counts just flow from the basic facts of genocide. That is not true. Genocide is a crime that can occur in peace as well as in armed conflict and the allegation of genocide did not put on us any burden of arguing whether or not an armed conflict existed at the time. As you all know, and from the Tadic trial and other trials, that the question of the extent of an armed conflict, when it occurred, whether the locality was, itself, had to be part of the armed conflict, all these are major issues which have nothing to do with genocide but have a lot to do with the 14 additional counts. That is just one example. There are all kinds of things we would now have to look up, that they knew about back in March of 1997 that we are finding out in January and February of 1998 that would have to change the entire picture of how we are approaching this case. With respect to the point that he said when he said that it might be better to substitute in the indictment document evidence as opposed to witnesses, first of all, he blacked out the name of any witness he did not want us to see, so we did not know who those witnesses were anyway. Secondly, we are not talking about an indictment but pre-trial discovery. You do not have to give us document re examples in the indictment. In fact, Mr Keegan wants it both ways: on the one hand he says, "we were very generous and gave you a lot of documentary and other evidence". On the other hand, he is saying, "because we did that we are entitled then to wait and amend the complaint later". He cannot have it both ways. When he refers to the fact that many domestic courts allow indictment of lesser included offences, I will stand on my brief on that. These crimes are not lesser, murder is not lesser than genocide. Just about everything in the added indictments could conceivably carry a life -- a penalty of life imprisonment, so it is not lesser at all, in fact, not even within the same realm. They come from different realms of international law. War crimes go back to the American Civil War and earlier. The Genocide Convention of 1949 post dates World War II. Genocide was something that was -- the word was invented in 1944 and was not part of the Nuremberg Tribunal but came with the resolution on genocide in 1948 and the Genocide Convention. These are all wildly different, they have nothing to do with each other. It is unfair that because we were asking for provisional release he did not want to tell us what the additional indictments are. How does that follow? It is illogical. If our client is sick and needs medical attention and we were trying to devote our attention to do that, what does that have to do with the ability of the Prosecution to disclose these additional counts that it has in mind? It really has nothing to do with that. Now let me just say a few words about Article 9, because I would like to rest on the brief and I thank the court for reading it and so I do not need to say much, but I would like to say, by way of rebuttal: Mr Keegan's approach to Article 9 is very simple and interesting. He says there is a purpose to Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Human Rights; what is that purpose? It does not say in Article 9 what the purpose is, but Mr Keegan knows what that purpose is. That purpose, Mr Keegan says, has to do with the initial arrest and detention. So he infers a purpose for Article 9 and then he uses that purpose to circumscribe what Article 9 says. These are equally fallacious steps. One, you infer purpose then use it to limit the meaning of the article. There is no justification for that. Article 9 of the covenant is entitled "liberty and security of person"; that does not talk about original arrest. The language of Article 9 clearly excludes what is going on here. Eleanor Roosevelt, at the time Article 9 was drafted in 1950, the question was -- I will read the language of paragraph 2, for those who would like to know what we are talking about here: "Anyone who is arrested shall be informed at the time of arrest of the reasons for his arrest and shall be promptly informed of any charges against him." "Any charges against him", is the key phrase. Now the question is, what does, "any charge against him" mean? The Philippine delegate in 1950 proposed we change that to, "shall be informed of the charges against him", figuring that whatever the charges were, the person should be informed of them. Mrs Roosevelt objected to that. She said -- this was summarised by Mrs Roosevelt at the time: it seemed better to her: "Not to replace 'any charges' by the words 'the charges', as the former text (that is the 'any charges') more nearly met the requirement that the right of the person to know all the charges against made him, whatever they were, should be protected." Now, Dr Kovacevic, when he was arrested on January 10 1997, had a right to know what all the charges were against him. Any of the charges, all the charges. He had a right to know that. Mr Keegan now admits that all the facts were in his possession to enumerate those charges and, of course, if we look at the Karadzic indictment we will see a list of similar charges drawn up two years before Dr Kovacevic's indictment. On far fewer facts they were able to come up with roughly the same thing. Dr Kovacevic had a right to know what all the charges were against him at the time he was arrested. Mr Keegan knew what the charges were, but he did not -- but he chose not to disclose them until six months later. If that is not a literal violation of a Human Rights Covenant, Article 9, I do not know what is. You cannot get round it by positing a purpose that does not exist in this thing to try to narrow the scope. The court is charged -- I am sure there is no argument about this -- with upholding the provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Human Rights. That is like a constitutional document that supersedes anything that is going on here, including our internal Rules. I think Mr Keegan has not made a dent in the specific arguments that I made that Article 9 applies here. They apply for very good reasons because otherwise the Prosecution can use tactics that are distinctly unfair, not just because it makes the trial unfair -- that is another narrowing point, I will conclude with that. It is not just that the trial maybe unfair, but we -- you and I -- we all enjoy human rights in addition to the right to a fair trial. Dr Kovacevic has human rights as a person presumed to be innocent. All this time that he is in the detention centre he still has the human rights. He had the human right of Article 9 and he has all the human rights of the International Covenant. They do not just depend on whether a fair trial comes later in time. They exist at the moment. At the moment he was arrested he was deprived of his human right under Article 9 to be informed of any charges against him. I will now turn over to Mr Vucicevic, unless there are any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution has basically, in the second part of the argument, attempted to emasculate the new Rule 50. They suggest that Rule 50 should be interpreted to effect, give the same lack of legal defence to the accused before this Trial Chamber, basically his interpretation would like to silence defence, were the meaning of the Article 50 as it is drafted now calls that leave to amend shall be by motion and everybody knows that the business of the court in deciding on the motion is not only to hear whether or not application for leave is timely -- which we heard it is not -- but also to hear whether or not the standards for confirmation are met. If the Prosecution has been willing to turn the supporting evidence willingly on the motion for provisional release and has turned it now, anticipating that this will be a hearing under new Rule 50, it is just plain unfair to allow them even to pedal back to say that they were given the supporting material. If this is Trial Chamber is going to accept such an argument, that would mean that this would and should be an ex parte hearing again, as it used to be before the amendment. However, we fully realise that embodiment, if the new Rule 50 gives right to Defence to point out to the inconsistencies in the evidence that the Prosecutor is adducing to support the indictment. The Prosecutor has repeatedly said that the standard of proof on the indictment is prima facie case or reasonable suspicion. We do not challenge the standard. This learned Chamber knows those standards. What the new Rule 50 has given the Defence is the right to challenge the evidence which does not rise to such a level; that gives us the right to comment and point to the inconsistencies of the witnesses. To Witness C, for example, being -- his statement being given twice, once being given early, which the Prosecution must have must have had for two years, where the sighting of Dr Kovacevic was not reported in the concentration, detention camp, and the statement of Witness C that was taken on July 18, where, supposedly, on one short page, the same witness has remembered Dr Kovacevic. That is the only thing that ties up Dr Kovacevic to the whole affair. The question is such an inconsistency and especially up on the massive publication that it happened and lack of the due diligence on behalf of the Prosecutor would certainly cause the Trial Chamber to give life to the new Rule 50 and if it all is timely and if it all is proper, after considering the whole indictment -- I would only say in the alternative the Trial Chamber might give the Prosecutor the chance to call such a witness to explain consistencies which are lethal to his testimony, even to substantiate the standard of a -- a minimal standard, such a prima facie case. I would go back, your Honours, on the different standard. In order to substantiate count on genocide, it has to be a plan in the first few paragraphs of the amended -- or let us put it, proposed amended indictment, are talking about a plan. The only fact indicating a plan, it is the testimony in Tadic's case where the Prosecutor examining Witness P, as in Peter, where, in direct leading language -- and we put it in our brief. I would just like, for the importance of this moment, to cite it: "The Prosecutor: who was it that said in 1992 that the upper tolerable limit on the presence of Muslims in Krajina would be 2 per cent?" That is the Prosecutor testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In 92 this was said by the president of the crisis committee Radislav Brjanin." Who was earlier disclosed to having been a president of the crisis committee in Banja Luka, not in Prijedor. This is all evidence of the plan. When we, your Honours, look at the evidence of the plan through testimony of other witnesses, because they were rather talkative in explaining witness Semenovic, witness Mujadzic, witness Merkal; as we pointed out first, there was no plan. Secondly, there were attempts, mutual attempts by all parties and politicians in Prijedor, more than any other area in Bosnia Herzegovina to avert the civil war. They were meeting and talking with each other before the political power takeover was carried out by the Serbian politicians. There was negotiations to avert a war, armed conflict. They were going on later. Federal policeman in federal Yugoslavia, who was very high-ranking, Mr Merkal testified that after takeover of power he met with Mr Drljaca, some other officers, where Mr Drljaca -- there is some confusion as to language, but it seems to me that he testified that Mr Drljaca was introduced as a Minister of Police. Another witness testified that Mr Drljaca was introduced -- that he got the appointment as assistant deputy Minister of Police. That, your Honours, in and of itself is very important, because the Prosecutor is defeating his own assertion that there was a superior authority, because the superior authority under the international customary law -- and the precedent that we have so far, going from the amasitar down to Lieutenant Kelly and Captain Merdana, committed the first, and the second being acquitted, of the war crimes in Vietnam, clearly established that this superior authority is applicable only to the commanders that have a high degree of control, military control. They can order their troops to sacrifice, order their men to sacrifice their life upon an order. Then there is no such authority ever being placed under the law. I am suggesting as a matter of law, the Prosecutor is on extremely shaky factual evidence trying to lead the Trial Chamber to extend a law that has never been extended so far. In order to allow him, he is asking you: "Please tell us, Defence, I would rather have my indictment without the facts". That would be contrary to what the due process of law is and interpreting Article 50 I think we all have to bear in mind the due process in law means fair and level playing-field. The defendant would be denied that. In terms of the facts, on the superior authority, your Honours, the Prosecutor is suggesting the town of Kosarac was a peaceful population that was levelled to the ground by a military attack of local military commanding by Dr Kovacevic. That would be his conclusion to invite you to support this indictment. However, in Tadic case -- and I believe some of the evidence was heard in that case by Judge Vohrah, if I am not mistaken. Colonel Selak, who was a chief logistics officer in the Fifth Corps, sitting in Banja Luka. There was a Yugoslav army retreating from Zagreb and made the headquarters in Banja Luka. He testified upon receiving reports in the headquarters on military activities at Kosarac, that he knew that the officers of such a corps were receiving ammunition supplies and salaries from general staff in Belgrade. I cannot surmise that a doctor from a small town, it is going to have any power to satisfy the prima facie standard on superior authority to be commanding, as one other witness testified, I believe, that is Mr Semenovic, it was told that was the strongest army corps in that part of Europe, meaning that they had at their disposal 34,000 soldiers. Just their facts missing there and all those gaping holes in the evidence are not supporting the logic. They are all being done and they are all being made by the Prosecution's witnesses on statements and testimony under oath. There is another major problem here, your Honours. That is how could we reconcile such a great reliance on the Crisis Staff. In the supporting material, some of us who had lived in a period of "enlightenment" in Tito's Yugoslavia where the self-management was created. Such self management has percolated down to the municipal levels. Did it mean anything? Not this Trial Chamber, but you know the other Trial Chambers, just as far as yesterday there was an expert testifying that there was no democracy there, there was no totalitarianism. I respectfully suggest that the western bankers and the governments have bought the Trojan horse of democracy in Yugoslavia, but it was nothing but the tripartite structure -- party, police and the military -- that divided up the spoils of the foreign investments. When the foreign investments stopped pouring in, the people who did not receive an opportunity to develop tolerance and respect for rule of law to a mutual productive work, to respect each other human being interacting properly, all of a sudden, in a poverty created, because there was no giveaways, they started this war. Your Honours, the mistake is the mistake that western bankers made by recognising self-management on a various level democracy, should not be a pretext that this Trial Chamber should take to implore superior authority just because these crisis committees existed. The Prosecutor in their supporting material indicated nothing that was direction from Mr Stakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. It seems we are now entering the realm of argument about the merits which would be more appropriately addressed, would it not, at the trial. At this stage we are merely seeking to determine whether we should amend the indictment. It seems to me that this sort of detail is not going to assist us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that comment, your Honour. The only thing I was attempting to do was to point out to standard of evidence which is not reach to go the probable suspicion. That was a suspicion the Crisis Staff had authority. Another point there, there was not a single fact in the amended indictment that Dr Kovacevic had any authority on the Crisis Staff and that he had been tied up to any of the acts that amended indictment is accusing him of. Your Honour, I am not talking -- I refer to it in our brief -- to facts that do not rise -- because what -- I will finish on this note: the Prosecutor is using interchangeably standard terminology under the international law but he is also using the term "ethnic cleansing". "Ethnic cleansing" is inflammatory and it is prejudicial to my client, because ethnic cleansing does not exist in the Statute, in any of the elements of the crime under the Statute. It does not exist in Genocide Convention or in the international customary law. "Ethnic cleansing" is a misnomer used only to convict and give more or less presumption of guilt to a Serbian side of this conflict for certain acts which should be adjudicated here. Therefore, a term carries such a significant stigma in and of itself that I ask this Trial Chamber to bar usage of such a term because it is not generic; it is wholesale; it does not describe anything; it is conclusary, it is judgmental. That is basically what the Prosecutor had used in order to support all of the crimes against humanity. All the crimes against humanity he is charging they have to have superior authority and all those elements to tie my client. With all due respect, your Honours, there was no intent specific to Mr Kovacevic that has been presented to make a prima facie case. There was no showing that he had command authority. There was no showing that has risen to prima facie that he had personally done any of this. Therefore, your Honours, I ask you to strike the counts based on genocide laws and the laws against humanity as far as the crimes that are grave breaches of Geneva Conventions and violation of the laws and customs of war, those crimes are not available to the Prosecutor charging a participant who was a member of insurgency in a civil war. The laws that are before you, if this were to be interpreted, if this were to be accepted, it is a cardinal violation of the principle crimine senalege, because on twice, two reports, Secretary-General has indicated, first, in adoption of the Statute for the Yugoslavia Tribunal and second, for adoption of the Rwanda Tribunal, has indicated that such principles should be respected. Moreover, the Secretary-General's report in adoption of the Rwanda Tribunal said explicitly, this is for the first time the common Article 3 has been written in as the Article 4 of Rwanda Tribunal. Therefore, by clear implication that article is not Yugoslavia Tribunal. There is a difficulty here and that is the Appeals Chamber in Tadic's case has interpreted that common article of the Geneva Conventions, Article 3 is a part of the Article 3 of the Statute for Yugoslavia, of this Tribunal. Well, that was not complete and full analysis because basic analysis was that that was international war, because those were the facts that were argued by the parties. However, the point of each was not considered. There were three parties to the war; there was Bosnian Muslim, Bosnian Serbs that were engaged in a civil war, and there was Yugoslav national army versus Bosnian Muslim and there was international war. If you do not look clearly to the facts, and only then we decide to make a pronouncement of the law, then we are going to make not only injustice to my client but we are going to set up international law which is not going to be fair. There is also indicia that such an interpretation of the law was incorrect and it is not bound on this Trial Chamber, based on the pronouncements of the International Court of Justice, international law, presidential value, all the cases, it is not strongly viewed as persuasive. What had happened; the Appeals Chamber accepted in preparation of Article 3, in trying to interpret the legislative history of post facto discussions in the Security Council, which consists of 15 members, three great powers have found a proper -- after adoption of the language, to make comments that such a language which was never on the face of the text, which will incorporate common Article 3. In domestic jurisdiction perhaps that would not have been so strongly considered but in 1966, even so, that common Article 3 has been incorporated by Security Council in the Rwanda Tribunal. International Law Commission; permanent member state delegates could not agree whether or not this incorporation of Article 3 is a part of the international customary law or not, based on this, the states that make the United Nations are not only three great powers have spoken. This could not be customary international law. Therefore, I respectfully ask you to deny amendments alleging violations of grave breaches of Geneva Conventions and violations of customs of war because they are not premised upon the acceptable law. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Keegan, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would just mention a few points with respect to the aspect, the argument with respect to Article 9(2) and the purpose of that Article, the commentary to the International Covenant makes it quite clear that the purpose of that article is the question of arbitrary arrest and detention. It goes on to say that the notification requirement in Article 9(2) itself relates only to the stage of arrest, not to the stage of detention or, in fact, thereafter. It is a question of notification, so that the person is above all in a position to make use of their right to remand under Article 9(4); that is, be in a position to challenge. In fact, the European Commission on Human Rights, in deliberating a case brought under Article 5 of the European Convention of Human Rights -- which is, of course, analagous, in fact the wording is almost exactly the same to Article 9 -- requiring again notification of any charges at the time of arrest. The European Commission on Human Rights found that Article 5(2), which is again the counter to Article 9(2), neither requires that the necessary information be in a particular form nor that it consists of a complete list of the charges held against the arrested person. The European Commission -- I believe a copy has been provided to your Honour of that case, as well as the commentaries to the Convention. It is not an issue that relates to the question of amendments of indictment in a case, which is what we are here about. Mr D'Amato, of course, is right that many of the charges in the amendment have discrete elements or aspects which are separate; the questions of characterisation of conflict, attack on a civilian population, whether it was widespread or systematic, et cetera. Those are just a part of the consideration. The focus of the Defence response was the question of investigation of the accused's involvement; that relates, as I understand it, as to which actions he did or did not undertake during the relevant period of time. That does flow from the basic set of facts and circumstances as I suggested. While, yes, there will be legal research necessary that was not necessary for the charge of genocide and perhaps the commission of experts -- hiring of experts by the Defence for particular legal questions, the basic question of their right to investigate in the issue of exculpatory evidence can flow from the same facts they have been investigating, and therefore it is a question of how much further time would be necessary. As to the question of Rule 50, the Office of the Prosecutor takes its reading of the Rules on its face. The problem of importing a process for contesting the confirmation of an indictment by the Defence would necessitate, in fact, we believe, a whole series of additional regulations in requirement by the Trial Chambers. If we engage in the same rights that accused has pursuant to Rule 72 under Rule 50 does that then obviate the rights of the accused under Rule 72, if they made use of them under Rule 50, or would they get to do them twice? What type of interventions would be necessary? Having fractured my leg twice, and maybe not being enough, I am about to stick my neck out and talk a bit about British Law now. It is my understanding that, in the UK, as well as many other systems, the modern trend is away from lengthy committal hearings, which would be the analogy here because of the determination that they have little effect on the right to a fair trial of an accused, given the rights of an accused at a trial itself. That is, I believe, the modern trend in the UK and Australia, other common law jurisdictions. In some civil law jurisdictions, the right of an accused is limited to written objections to an indictment or its analagous document at the stage that that document becomes viable. The question here really is: how do we read Rule 50 in light of the other Rules that already exist in this Tribunal? We believe that the only appropriate reading of Rule 50 in light of Article 19 and Rule 47 and the subsequent rights of accused under Rule 72, we believe this whole thing, of course, has to be pinned on the question that the accused is not losing any right to contest an indictment. Those rights have always existed under the Rules of the Tribunal and will continue to exist under Rule 72. All that Rule 50 did was change the mechanism for the confirmation of indictment in the situation where an accused has made an initial appearance. It did not change any of the standards of confirmation or the processes. The accused has always had the right to contest and will have the right to contest an indictment post-confirmation under Rule 72. That is why we believe Rule 50 does not envisage the type of process we have had here today, where the Defence will argue the evidence which would then require the Prosecution to re-argue and end up in what we refer to in our reply as, "a mini trial".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr Keegan, you would accept that the court has to judge -- the Tribunal Chamber has to judge the matter with respect to the necessity for a fair and expeditious trial. That is a matter we have to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There is no question that the rights, under Article 21, of an accused to a trial without undue delay is a fundamental right. That is a fundamental right in every system. As I indicated earlier, we believe that the question of what is an undue delay is relevant to the requirements of each particular system and, in fact, to each particular case. It must be judged within that context. The underlying question in every system, when this issue is reached, is: will the amendment or the change in the indictment result in injustice or, as we termed it, substantially prejudice the accused to the right to a fair trial. If the answer is no, we believe leave to amend should be granted and the question of delay is merely one factor to be considered within the large scheme of the right of both the international community and the accused to a fair trial. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall --

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: May I have one minute to rebut?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have heard enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: These were new points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we heard the points and got your point. We will adjourn for 20 minutes and we will consider this amendment and consider what course to take. (3.48 pm) (A short break) (4.10 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have considered this motion. We have come to this conclusion: in our judgement, it is far too late in the day to amend an indictment as substantially as is being proposed. We think that if this amendment were allowed it would not be possible to hold a fair trial and certainly not an expeditious one. Accordingly, we refuse the motion and we shall give our reasons in writing in due course. Mr Vucicevic and Mr D'Amato, you have a motion to strike parts of the amendment. Do you want to pursue that?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We appreciate the fact that you read it, considered it and we would sooner drop that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the only matter which is not disputed is that the name of the co-accused should be removed. I take it, Mr Keegan, that that will happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That being so, are there any other matters to be raised in open session before we go into closed session and conduct a status conference, as we said we would?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, upon hearing the ruling of this Trial Chamber, if you would give us 30 seconds to a minute, maximum, just to consider, because there was another motion and there was a motion to strike original indictment. When your Honour spoke, you indicated whether or not we would like to strike certain portion of the amended indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I just waived that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think Mr D'Amato just dealt with that, in fact. Perhaps you would like to have a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to have a word with Mr D'Amato before having a final one on that one. There was a language difficulty here, in my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you, 30 seconds. (Pause). Thank you, your Honour. My original statement stands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other matters to be dealt with in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we will go into closed session to have a status conference on this trial.
